title: "Wow, 2450% return in 10y". But... 181% is forward-tested (in 16 months!)
author: insights-center
selftext:
I created an AI algorithm that allocates and picks stocks from within the SPY and other screeners based on the principles of Benjamin Graham in The Intelligent Investor, but with a twist to better adapt to modern conditions. Long story short, the backtest returns 2550% in 10 years and 181% in the 16-month forward test. Oh, but there's more. I actually applied the algorithm to one of my trading accounts and had it return 115% in a year! If you are looking for some specific numbers relating to the performance, you'll find them below. I'm open to any questions too.

[10 year graph modelling algorithm performance v SPY with key figures included](https://preview.redd.it/yokj4zg6vhih1.png?width=923&format=png&auto=webp&s=07bf65406e81511d207122b3b0434744b8221a6b)

[All relevant numbers to the algorithm](https://preview.redd.it/oul5n62hwhih1.png?width=644&format=png&auto=webp&s=6f4aacc21a6b3c08882068c3f1fe1fcb00a8510a)

comments.author: Fynca
comments.body:
Interesting results. The key question is whether the backtest used the historical SPY constituents available at each point in time. Using today’s members could introduce significant survivorship bias.

I’d also want to see performance against SPY over the same periods, maximum drawdown, turnover, concentration, transaction costs and monthly returns. Was the algorithm changed at any point after reviewing the forward-test results?

A 16-month forward test is encouraging, but these details would help show whether the edge is robust or mainly driven by the recent market regime.

replies.author: insights-center
replies.body: You're in luck. The changing SPY holdings (there are some data misalignments, though - not more than a week - but it hasn't had a large impact on the final graph; I calculated a few percent error bound overall) were accounted for, and you can find your SPY benchmark data in the second screenshot of the data. Let me know if you have more questions.

replies.author: Fynca
replies.body:
Thanks, that helps. The main thing I’d still want to clarify is whether the model, screening rules and all parameters were frozen before the 16-month forward test began.

If anything was adjusted during that period, did you restart the forward-test clock? That distinction probably matters more than the small SPY data misalignment.

replies.author: insights-center
replies.body: Sorry I missed that question. No changes were made in that 16-month period, hence the forward test and actual live test.

comments.author: Antitesla
comments.body: Drawdown 47%? It’s seems to be grid bot. Any grid bot have ability to loose all deposit. But snp or gold is a good option for this strategy.

replies.author: insights-center
replies.body: It doesn’t have the ability to lose all holdings, once the market loses momentum, it trips holdings. Once it picks back up, it invests more

comments.author: Interesting_Gold_792
comments.body:
The 16-month frozen forward test is the part that makes this much more interesting.

What I’d really want to isolate now is where the edge is actually coming from.

Have you run an attribution test separating:

\- the stock-selection model,  
\- the momentum/regime filter that moves the portfolio in and out,  
\- and the allocation/sizing logic?

For example, if you keep the exact same momentum/exposure rules but replace the AI stock picks with equal-weight SPY constituents or a simpler ranking model, how much of the excess return remains?

The \~47% max drawdown also makes me curious whether most of the performance is coming from a few high-beta periods rather than a consistently positive edge.

I think that decomposition would be more informative than the headline CAGR by itself.

replies.author: insights-center
replies.body: To start, the outperformance comes from all three pillars of stock selection, market timing, and position sizing. I can give you details on how each of those pillars works if you are curious. I can't give you a definite answer on which pillar is doing the "heavy lifting", but I would say it probably comes from the stock selection, since that is based on the market timing in a lot of ways. Second, removing that AI selection system and substituting with an equal-weight system would absolutely result in significantly lower gains, yet still beating the market by a considerable margin. I don't have exact numbers for that, but I guarantee you that would be the result of that test given my knowledge of the holdings throughout that time period and my own live testing. Third, good performance is spread out, although the strongest was during strong bull runs. Yes, high-beta periods can carry the model, but other periods still significantly contribute. Let me know if you have any other questions.
